questions.q: Name two cable-based and two wireless communication technologies mentioned in the NCERT textbook for Class 11 Home Science Chapter 6.
questions.a: Cable-based: landline telephone, personal computer without internet (implied wired LAN/Ethernet). Wireless: radio, microwave, satellite wireless telephony, Bluetooth. A wrong answer (e.g., listing "mobile phone" as cable-based or "optical fibre" as wireless) reveals the student is confusing the *device* with the *transmission medium* — they must learn to ask: "Does the signal travel through a physical wire/fibre or through air/space?"

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Bluetooth is classified as a wireless technology even though it operates only over very short distances (typically 10 metres).
questions.a: Bluetooth uses low-power radio frequency (RF) waves in the 2.4 GHz ISM band to transmit voice and data between devices without any physical connector; the short range is a design choice (low transmit power ~1 mW) to save battery and avoid interference, not a wired connection. A wrong answer citing "it connects devices so it must be wired" or "short range means cable" shows the student equates *physical proximity* with *guided media* — they need to distinguish "no cable between endpoints" (wireless) from "short cable" (still cable-based).

questions.q: A rural extension officer wants to send weekly agricultural advisories to 500 farmers across three villages separated by hilly terrain. Compare cable-based (optical fibre) and wireless (community radio + SMS) options on four parameters: initial infrastructure cost, time to deploy, reach to illiterate users, and reliability during monsoon. Which would you recommend and why?
questions.a: Optical fibre: high initial cost (₹50–80 lakh for trenching/ducting in hills), 6–12 months deployment, requires smartphones/literacy for SMS/app, vulnerable to landslides cutting cables. Community radio (FM transmitter ~₹5 lakh) + SMS gateway: low cost, 2–3 weeks deployment, radio reaches illiterate farmers via voice, SMS works on basic phones; monsoon degrades FM slightly but rarely cuts it entirely. Recommendation: wireless combo — it matches the terrain, literacy profile, and urgency. A wrong recommendation of fibre ignores the *contextual fit* principle: technology choice is not about "which is faster" but "which works *here*."

questions.q: Analyse the statement: "Cable-based technologies are always more secure than wireless technologies because signals are confined to the physical medium." Identify two scenarios where this generalisation fails at the senior secondary level.
questions.a: The statement fails when: (1) Physical tapping — an attacker with access to a junction box or splice point can split an optical fibre and intercept light with a bend-coupler without cutting the link; (2) Compromised endpoints — if the router/server at either end is hacked (malware, weak password), the medium's confinement is irrelevant. A student who only cites "wireless signals spread in air so easier to sniff" misses that *security is end-to-end*, not medium-dependent; they need to think beyond the propagation medium to the full threat model.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "For a school in a dense urban neighbourhood, a wired Ethernet LAN is always superior to Wi-Fi for student learning activities." Consider pedagogical, health, and equity dimensions, not just bandwidth.
questions.a: The claim is *partially valid but incomplete*. Wired LAN gives consistent high bandwidth, low latency, no RF interference — good for video editing, coding exams. But: (1) Pedagogical — Wi-Fi enables mobility (group work in corridors, science labs, library), BYOD inclusivity for students without Ethernet ports; (2) Health — no credible evidence of harm from 2.4/5 GHz Wi-Fi at regulatory power levels (ICNIRP/WHO), so "health risk" is a misconception; (3) Equity — wiring every desk costs ₹2–3 lakh/classroom vs ₹30k for enterprise APs; funds saved can buy devices for low-income students. A one-sided "wired is better" answer ignores the *total learning ecosystem*; a balanced evaluation weighs trade-offs against the school's actual constraints.

questions.q: Design a communication technology plan for a mobile health van serving 20 tribal hamlets in a forested district (no grid power, no cellular coverage, 50 km from nearest town). Specify: (a) primary backbone technology, (b) last-mile access technology, (c) power strategy, (d) one fallback method. Justify each choice in one sentence.
questions.a: (a) Primary backbone: VSAT (satellite) terminal on van roof — works anywhere with sky view, no ground infrastructure. (b) Last-mile: Wi-Fi hotspot (2.4 GHz) from van to hamlet community centre — connects villagers' basic phones/tablets without SIM cards. (c) Power: 500 W solar panels + 2 kWh lithium battery on van — silent, renewable, survives cloudy days. (d) Fallback: Store-and-forward — van downloads/uploads batches when it reaches town with 4G coverage. A poor answer picks "optical fibre" or "4G dongle" ignoring the *no coverage/no power* constraints; the task tests whether the student can *synthesise* a fit-for-context stack from the building blocks.
